extension_policy: The new entries cover 1920–2000 with earlier roots; their spans end at the 2000 coverage limit. Later works appear as cited readings, historiographical sources and strand works. nodes.label: Laurentian & national tradition
nodes.date_label: Staple studies 1923–40 · Creighton 1937 · Lower 1946 · Careless 1954 · Centenary Series volumes 1964–85 · Berger's analysis 1976 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: English-Canadian historical writing that took the transcontinental nation-state as its frame, from the interwar years to the centennial. Its economic core is the staple approach: Innis's studies of the fur trade (1930) and cod fisheries (1940) read Canada's development through exports to imperial centres, an approach Watkins later called Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy. Creighton's Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) simplified and expanded Innis's thesis, making Montreal's merchants the 'spiritual fathers' of Confederation; his Macdonald biography followed. Liberal nationalists such as Lower and Underhill and conservative nationalists such as Creighton and Stacey disagreed politically while sharing the nation-state as the frame of reference. Careless offered a metropolitan interpretation (1954), which Donald Davis (1985) found indeterminate, and Morton asked in 1946 on what critical premises the established interpretations rested. The Canadian Centenary Series, from 1964, gathered national syntheses, including translated volumes by the Quebec historians Trudel and Ouellet. Cook's and Careless's 'limited identities' (1967, 1969) and the new regional history of Acadiensis (1971) challenged the frame, and Berger's Writing of Canadian History (1976) analysed the English-Canadian tradition as a historiographical subject. French-Canadian historians such as Michel Brunet pursued a rival national vision, treated under Quebec historiography.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Mackintosh, "Economic Factors in Canadian History" (1923); Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940); Creighton, The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) and John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955); Lower, Colony to Nation (1946); Underhill, In Search of Canadian Liberalism (1960); Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History" (1954); Morton, "Clio in Canada" (1946) and The Kingdom of Canada (1963); Canadian Centenary Series volumes by Morton (1964), Neatby (1966), Trudel (1973), Brown and Cook (1974), Ouellet (1980). Restatement: Watkins (1963). Analysis: Berger, The Writing of Canadian History (1976, 1986); Buckner (2000); Miville (2016). Critics: Cook (1967), Careless (1969), Buckner (1971), Davis (1985).
nodes.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not one school. The staple approach (political economy), Creighton's Laurentian narrative, liberal and conservative nationalisms, metropolitanism and the Centenary Series are distinct projects; roster inclusion is not membership. The label avoids 'Laurentian school': no checked source uses that phrase. French-Canadian and Quebec national historiography belongs to Quebec historiography: Trudel and Ouellet are named only in the Centenary Series strand, and the Creighton–Brunet comparison is carried by the relationship note, not the roster. Stacey (official history, external policy) is placed in Canadian military history and Political, international & national history; Stanley appears as a secondary row for The Birth of Western Canada. Critics appear as critics.

nodes.label: English-Canadian intellectual & cultural history
nodes.date_label: Berger 1970, 1976 · McKillop 1979 · Owram 1980, 1986 · cultural turn: McKay 1994, Vance 1997, Nelles 1999 · coverage through 2000; selected later readings
nodes.description: English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history studies how Canadians thought about empire, nation, religion, science and the state, and later how traditions, myths and public memories were made. Carl Berger's The Sense of Power (1970) examined imperialist ideas of Canadian character and mission and argued that Canadian imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism; his The Writing of Canadian History (1976) made English-Canadian historical writing itself a subject. A. B. McKillop, Marlene Shore and Doug Owram followed ideas into the university, social science, western expansion and the interwar 'service state'. Ramsay Cook's The Regenerators (1985) joined the field to religious history. Critics charged it with what Clarence Karr (1989) called a 'narrow, elitist, biographical methodology': group biographies of academics, journalists and clergy that said little about what most Canadians thought. Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979) had argued that a field anchored to nationalism left women almost invisible. From the 1990s a cultural history of invention and memory developed alongside it. Ian McKay's The Quest of the Folk (1994) showed tourism promoters and cultural producers refashioning Nova Scotians as a simple folk. Daniel Francis wrote on the 'imaginary Indian' and national myths, and Jonathan Vance on the memory of the First World War. H. V. Nelles, Keith Walden, E. A. Heaman and Ian Radforth studied pageants, exhibitions and royal tours, and Colin Coates and Cecilia Morgan the commemoration of heroines. Yvan Lamonde's social history of ideas in Quebec runs on a separate francophone track.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Berger, The Sense of Power (1970), The Writing of Canadian History (1976; 1986), Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983); Cook, The Maple Leaf Forever (1971), The Regenerators (1985); McKillop, A Disciplined Intelligence (1979), Matters of Mind (1994); Owram, Promise of Eden (1980), The Government Generation (1986); Shore, The Science of Social Redemption (1987); Litt (1992); Vipond (1992); Francis, The Imaginary Indian (1992), National Dreams (1997); McKay, The Quest of the Folk (1994); Vance, Death So Noble (1997); Walden (1997); Heaman, The Inglorious Arts of Peace (1999); Nelles, The Art of Nation-Building (1999); Coates and Morgan, Heroines and History (2002); Radforth, Royal Spectacle (2004); Igartua (2006). Critiques: Trofimenkoff, “Nationalism, Feminism & Canadian Intellectual History” (1979); Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” (1989). Comparisons: Lamonde, Histoire sociale des idées au Québec (2000); Lears, No Place of Grace (1981).
nodes.scope_note: English-Canadian by design; Quebec's histoire sociale des idées is a comparison (Lamonde). Intellectual history (ideas, intellectuals, the university) and cultural history (spectacle, myth, memory) are distinct strands with different methods. The religious strand is shared with Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada, postwar identity with Canada’s 1960s. Editorial observation, not a sourced claim: Indigenous people appear in this field mostly as settler representations (Francis, Heaman), which is a limit to flag in teaching. PhD evidence (2009–2026): engagement with the field's anchor scholars is steady (ratio 1.02; 1.14 in a fixed panel of 14 universities), while its older works are cited less; the classics are ageing, not the field. Owram's 'Intellectual History in the Land of Limited Identities' (JCS 24:3, 1989; abstract checked, not cited as a source) is a practitioner's self-assessment that also notes the field's nationalist roots and the differing methods of francophone and anglophone writers; it is not treated as a critique.

nodes.label: Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada
nodes.date_label: Allen, The Social Passion 1971 · Cook, The Regenerators 1985 · secularization debate: Gauvreau 1991, Marshall 1992 and 1993–94, Christie and Gauvreau 1996 · coverage through 2000; selected later readings
nodes.description: Historical writing on Christianity as a force in Canadian reform, culture and everyday life, and on whether and when Canada secularized. Its central argument came in 1985–96. Ramsay Cook’s The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social criticism as the sacred becoming secular, and David Marshall’s Secularizing the Faith (1992) followed Protestant clergy through a crisis of belief to the 1920s as “an era of drift”. Their critics attacked this as the secularization thesis. Michael Gauvreau’s The Evangelical Century (1991) argued that the evangelical creed adapted to Darwinism and higher criticism; Marshall replied in 1993–94 that attempts to dismiss secularization were premature. In A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996) Nancy Christie and Gauvreau argued that the Protestant churches reached their greatest cultural influence before 1940 and placed secularization after the Second World War. Behind the debate stands Richard Allen’s The Social Passion (1971), which made the social gospel central to the history of reform, though recent doctoral work cites it far less. Social histories of Protestant culture, Methodism, gender and leisure (Westfall, Semple, Marks) moved the question from doctrine to lay practice. Catholic history developed alongside: Hamelin and Gagnon’s synthesis of Quebec Catholicism, Perin on Rome, McGowan on Irish Toronto. Gauvreau later carried the revision into Quebec, tracing the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action (2005). Later work studies irreligion in settler British Columbia (Marks 2017), distinguishes political from social secularization (Van Die) and treats religion as a vehicle of the liberal order (Christie). Moral reform as regulation belongs to a neighbouring field.

Comparison: Brown, The Death of Christian Britain (2001).
nodes.scope_note: A research field containing a debate. “Secularization thesis” is the name its critics gave to Cook’s and Marshall’s accounts (Laverdure’s 1998 review of Christie and Gauvreau); Marshall defended the concept in 1993–94. Both sides appear as historians. Catholic and Protestant histories have different genealogies; Irish Catholic history (McGowan, Perin) stays here. The Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution (Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue, Gauvreau 2005) has its main home in Quebec historiography, reached from here by the contribution edge crr_rel_04. Moral reform as regulation (Valverde) is placed in Moral regulation.

nodes.label: Liberal order framework
nodes.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · coverage through 2000; selected later readings
nodes.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures, and Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).
nodes.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Bannister, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.

nodes.label: Moral regulation
nodes.date_label: International roots (Corrigan 1981; Corrigan and Sayer 1985) · Kinsman 1987 · Valverde and Weir 1988 · Valverde 1991 · critiques 1994–97 · Strange and Loo 1997 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Studies how morality, sexuality, health and conduct were made objects of governance by reformers, churches, professions, courts and the state, and how regulation shaped the selves of the regulated. The concept came into historical sociology through Philip Corrigan's work (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch (1985), which treated English state formation as a cultural revolution; Ruonavaara describes their framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with Marxist theory. In Canada, Mariana Valverde and Lorna Weir offered preliminary remarks on moral regulation in Resources for Feminist Research (1988), and Valverde's The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) argued that Protestant social-purity reformers were not simply repressive and that they linked sexual health to racial purity and slum clearance. Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987), and later The Canadian War on Queers (2010, with Gentile), examined sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against gays and lesbians. Studies of contraception and eugenics (McLaren), women, girls and the law (Backhouse, Lévesque, Dubinsky, Strange, Sangster), welfare and single mothers (Little), and postwar normality (Adams, Gleason) widened the field. Adams tied moral regulation to state formation through venereal-disease policy, and Strange and Loo surveyed law and moral regulation from 1867 to 1939 (1997). Critics reformulated the concept: Dean (1994) recast Corrigan's account through Foucault's governmentality, and Ruonavaara (1997) rejected a monolithic, state-only project. The liberal order framework (McKay 2000) is a separate entry, closer to a history of capitalism.

Critiques and reformulations: Dean (1994); Hunt (1997, 1999); Ruonavaara (1997); Valverde, Diseases of the Will (1998). Extension: Sangster, Regulating Girls and Women (2001); Kinsman and Gentile, The Canadian War on Queers (2010).
nodes.scope_note: A research field, international in its theory and Canadian in most of its historical work. The liberal order framework is a separate project, 'closer to history of capitalism' (user, 2026-10-12); state formation (Curtis) is shared ground, not membership. Feminist legal and sexual history overlaps Canadian women's & gender history; youth and normality overlaps Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Roster inclusion does not mean a scholar adopts the moral-regulation framework.

nodes.label: Canadian working-class history
nodes.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · coverage through 2000, selected later works
nodes.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.

nodes.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) are treated mainly in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his main entry is Liberal order framework.

nodes.label: Canadian women's & gender history
nodes.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier women writers of history: Machar, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Neatby, Ormsby, Daveluy, as recovered in Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (1950). Cook and Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere (1976); Strong-Boag, The Parliament of Women (1976); Kealey, ed., A Not Unreasonable Claim (1979). Collectif Clio, L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982; Quebec Women, 1987); Prentice et al., Canadian Women: A History (1988). Pierson, "They're Still Women After All" (1986); Danylewycz, Taking the Veil (1987); Strong-Boag, The New Day Recalled (1988); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la crise (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993). Debate: Pierson (1991); Parr (1995); Sangster (1995, 1996); Iacovetta and Kealey (1996); Dubinsky and Marks (1996); Lévesque (1997); Sangster's retrospect (2011). Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996); McPherson, Morgan and Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts (1999); Parr, Domestic Goods (1999); Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs (2000); Christie, Engendering the State (2000). Comparison: Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" (1980); Perry, On the Edge of Empire (2001). Extension: Fahrni (2005), Campbell (2009), Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018), Bienvenue and Dorais, eds., Profession historienne? (2023).
nodes.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in Quebec historiography, where 91% of its citing PhDs sit; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to Quebec historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with Moral regulation; childhood and family with Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in Canadian working-class history, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (after 2000).
strands.works: Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Prentice, “Laying Siege to the History Professoriate” (1997); Cleverdon (1950); Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018)

strands.title: Gender history and women's history: the dichotomies exchange
strands.focus: Whether gender history extends or displaces women’s history. Pierson’s 1991 essay opens on the turn to deconstruction and Scott. Sangster’s “Beyond Dichotomies” (1995), by her own later account, protested “the hierarchy being established between a superior gender history and a ‘limited’ women’s history”; replies by Dubinsky and Marks and by Iacovetta and Kealey defended gender history against her dichotomy, and she answered (1996). She later found the exchange “not very satisfying, with discussants sometimes talking at cross-purposes”. The replies were not read; their positions are not characterised further.

nodes.description: Studies children, adolescents and families in Canadian history, and the reformers, experts, courts, schools and welfare programmes that sought to shape them. Neil Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) traced the reformers who pursued social improvement through children. Parr's study of British child immigrants (1980) and her collection Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982), Rooke and Schnell's history of child rescue and the welfare state (1983) and Bradbury's family economies of industrial Montreal (1993) tied the field to family and labour history. The 1990s brought studies of maternal and infant welfare (Comacchio 1993), the baby boom (Owram 1996), youth and the making of heterosexuality (Adams 1997) and psychology and the 'normal' family (Gleason 1999). Francophone work examined family allowances and compulsory schooling (Marshall 1998), juvenile reform schools (Ménard 2003) and the medicalization of motherhood (Baillargeon 2004). Comacchio treats adolescence as a sociohistorical construction (2006); Myers studies girls, the courts and the policing of children in Montreal and beyond (2006, 2019). John Bullen's review essay on recent approaches to child-welfare history (1985) is the one early critique found. Historians also ask how young people's own experience can be recovered: Sutherland on adult memories of childhood (1992), and Gleason's critique of 'agency traps' (2016). The field overlaps with women's and gender history and with moral regulation; residential schooling of Indigenous children is treated primarily in the Native–newcomer entry.

nodes.label: Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada
nodes.date_label: Ward 1978 · Avery 1979 · Abella and Troper 1982 · Perin 1983 · Anderson 1991 · Walker on race and the law 1997 · Backhouse 1999 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Studies immigration, ethnic communities, racism and the state in Canada: immigrant workers and their reception, ethnic identity, and the legal and spatial making of racial categories. The field expanded from the late 1970s. Ward's White Canada Forever (1978) traced west-coast prejudice against Asian residents and the discriminatory policies it produced; Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979) examined European immigrant workers and labour radicalism; Abella and Troper studied Canada and the Jews of Europe, 1933–48 (1982). Perin's 'Clio as an Ethnic' (1983) asked whether ethnic groups had been 'discovered' just when the state faced challenges such as Quebec nationalism. Studies of Toronto neighbourhoods (Harney, who co-founded the Multicultural History Society of Ontario in 1976), Italian migrants in Montreal (Ramirez), Chinese Montrealers (Helly), Quebec's immigration policy (Pâquet 1997), British Columbia politicians (Roy), Italian immigrants in postwar Toronto (Iacovetta) and Ukrainian-Canadian women (Swyripa) followed. Anderson (1987, 1991) treated 'Chinese' and 'Chinatown' as racial categories made through government practice and place, which a reviewer saw as moving beyond earlier studies of white prejudice; Walker's Supreme Court case studies (1997) and Backhouse's Colour-Coded (1999) traced racism through law. Black Canadian history, including Black migration and immigration control, is a separate entry. Post-2000 work turned to Cold War reception and citizenship (Iacovetta 2006; Bohaker and Iacovetta 2009).

nodes.label: Black Canadian history
nodes.date_label: Earlier work: Trudel on slavery in French Canada 1960 · Winks's survey 1971 · Walker's Black Loyalists 1976 · Calliste on sleeping car porters 1987 · Brand's oral history of Black working women 1991 · We're Rooted Here, African Canadian women's history 1994 · Walker's five orientations 1997 · Cahill–Walker Black Loyalist exchange 1999 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000, selected later works
nodes.description: Historical writing on people of African descent in Canada: slavery in New France and British North America, Black Loyalists and refugees, fugitive slaves and the settlements of Canada West, Black communities and churches, migration from the United States and the Caribbean, and racism in work, law and the state. Marcel Trudel documented slavery in French Canada (1960; dictionary 1990). After earlier work by Landon, Riddell and Trudel, Robin Winks's survey The Blacks in Canada (1971), which Walker reviewed critically, and James Walker's The Black Loyalists (1976), which put Black community at the centre; Winks credited it with ending the 'victims' school. From the late 1980s Agnes Calliste studied sleeping car porters and Caribbean migrants, Dorothy Williams Black Montreal, and Dionne Brand and the authors of We're Rooted Here (1994) Black women's history. In 1997 Walker sorted the historiography into five orientations by the role it gives Black people, from 'clients' of white philanthropy (Landon, Riddell) through 'victims' and 'achievers' to 'community' and 1990s 'survivors', and argued that community is the key. Barry Cahill called the Black Loyalists a scholars' myth that sidelined the enslaved (1999); Walker replied, placing his book in the civil-rights era. After 2000 the field grew around slavery (Cooper, Whitfield, Mackey), migration and labour (Mathieu), law (Barrington Walker) and Black Montreal (Austin, Mills), countering the image of Canada as a haven at the end of the Underground Railroad.

nodes.scope_note: A research field on people of African descent in Canada, defined by its subject, from slavery in New France to Black migration, community and racism. Created on the user's decision of 2026-10-12: it was a strand of Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada, and Walker's 1997 essay treats it as its own historiography. Its relation to immigration history is a comparison, not a hierarchy; works on Black migration and immigration control (Calliste 1993–94, Shepard 1997) are cross-referenced in that entry. Several roster people are treated mainly elsewhere (Trudel: Quebec historiography; Mills: Canada’s 1960s; Austin is also in Canada’s 1960s). Community and non-academic historians (Hill, Brand, Ruck, Mackey) are included because Walker's reading list and PhD bibliographies use them; Ruck and Forsythe are cited as community and participants' accounts. Indigenous slavery in New France (panis) is not covered; Rushforth's Bonds of Alliance (2012; 20 PhDs), whose title pairs Indigenous and Atlantic slaveries, is excluded from the counts because its Black-history content was not checked.

nodes.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
nodes.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · coverage through 2000, selected later works
nodes.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936); Ray, Indians in the Fur Trade (1974); Fisher, Contact and Conflict (1977); Van Kirk, “Many Tender Ties” (1980); Brown, Strangers in Blood (1980); Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976), Natives and Newcomers (1985), “The Historians’ Indian” (1986); Delâge, Le pays renversé (1985); Dickason, The Myth of the Savage (1984), Canada’s First Nations (1992); Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989), Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Brownlie and Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution” (1994); Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999). Later: Rutherdale (2002), Brownlie (2003), Raibmon (2005), Podruchny (2006), Lutz, Makúk (2008). Critics and alternatives: Sioui (1989), Paul, We Were Not the Savages (1993; 2000 edition), Stevenson [Wheeler], “The Othering of Indigenous History” (1998), LaRocque (1999); in the US, Fixico (2009) and S. A. Miller (2009).
nodes.scope_note: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework and do not adopt it, and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with Settler colonialism.

strands.title: Agency as alibi? An internal critique
strands.focus: Brownlie and Kelm (1994) criticised agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin 1990; Miller; Loo 1992): stressing Native agency exaggerated how far it became effective self-defence, trivialising the harm of colonial policy and serving as an ‘alibi’ for it. A critique within policy history, not of the fur-trade literature; targets known from a secondary source, essay unread.
strands.works: Robin Brownlie and Mary-Ellen Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution: Native Agency as Colonialist Alibi?” CHR 75:4 (December 1994): 543–56

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
strands.focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints: its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Fixico and S. Miller (2009, US) question ‘Indian–white relations’ as the premise of Indian history. Paul’s We Were Not the Savages (1993; the 2000 Fernwood edition is the one PhDs cite), subtitled ‘a Mi’kmaq perspective’, rejects the ‘savage’ category (title and subtitle only). Adams’s Prison of Grass (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official history, not a critique of this field, and Dickason is a member of the field. Trigger (1986) and Brownlie and Kelm (1994) are non-Indigenous critiques from inside. These are critics and alternatives, not members.
strands.works: Sioui (1989); Paul (1993; 2000 ed.); Stevenson [Wheeler] (Fall 1998); LaRocque (1999); Fixico (2009); S. A. Miller (2009)

strands.title: After 2000: the settler-colonial reading and its critics
strands.focus: Settler-colonial analysis reads reserves, schools and dispossession as a continuing structure. Greer replies that the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others, and that commercial penetration (the fur trade’s mode) and extractivism are other forms of invasion. Konishi records Indigenous scholars’ critiques of settler colonial studies. Extension only.
strands.works: Greer, “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (JCHA 2019); Konishi (2019)

nodes.label: Quebec historiography
nodes.date_label: Earlier national history (Groulx) · Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française founded 1946, its Revue from 1947 · Montreal and Laval schools 1950s–60s · Histoire du Québec contemporain 1979 · Rudin’s critique 1992 · coverage through 2000; selected later readings (Catholic Action revision 2002–05)
nodes.description: Historical writing on Quebec and French Canada, mostly in French, long organized around the nation, the Conquest of 1760 and the meaning of modernity. Lionel Groulx’s national history of French Canada closes what a francophone anthology calls the time of the ‘ancients’; Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française (1946) and its Revue (1947). In the 1950s historians at Montréal (Séguin, Frégault, Brunet) made the Conquest and its consequences their central problem. At Laval, Trudel wrote the history of New France, and Hamelin and Ouellet economic and social history, Ouellet in a conjunctural idiom indebted to Labrousse. Their agricultural-crisis thesis (1962) was contested by Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Dechêne, trained in the Annales milieu in France, wrote the social history of seventeenth-century Montreal (1974). After 1970 a modernist generation turned to contemporary, urban and industrial Quebec and to its whole population (Linteau, Durocher and Robert, 1979). Women’s history followed, from the Collectif Clio (1982) to Baillargeon (1991); Lévesque (1997) asked how far colleagues had integrated it. Behiels (1985) found the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60; Rouillard (1997) recorded a shift from reading it as rupture to turn. Ronald Rudin (1992, 1997) argued that the modernists’ search for a ‘normal’ society muted religion, rurality and ethnicity; Linteau and Fecteau replied (1995). Bouchard and Lamonde (2000) close the period; after 2000, Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue and Gauvreau traced the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Groulx, Histoire du Canada français depuis la découverte (1950); IHAF (1946) and RHAF (1947); Séguin, La “nation canadienne” et l’agriculture (thesis 1947; 1970); Frégault, La guerre de la Conquête (1955); Brunet, La présence anglaise et les Canadiens (1958); Trudel, L’esclavage au Canada français (1960) and Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (1963–); Hamelin, Économie et société en Nouvelle-France (1960); Ouellet and Hamelin, “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada” (1962); Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850 (1966); Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Wallot, Un Québec qui bougeait (1973); Dechêne, Habitants et marchands (1974); Savard (1974); Gagnon, Le Québec et ses historiens (1978); Linteau, Durocher and Robert, Histoire du Québec contemporain (1979; 1986); Collectif Clio (1982); Linteau, “La nouvelle histoire du Québec vue de l’intérieur” (1983); Behiels, Prelude to Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (1985); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989) and “Réflexions sur l’histoire des femmes dans l’histoire du Québec” (1997); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la Crise (1991); Rudin, “Revisionism and the Search for a Normal Society” (1992; French 1995) and Making History in Twentieth-Century Quebec (1997); Linteau and Fecteau (1995); Dumont, Genèse de la société québécoise (1993); Dickinson and Young, A Short History of Quebec (1993 ed.); Bouchard (1996, 2000); Martel (1997); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997); Lamonde (2000). Later: Meunier and Warren, Sortir de la « grande noirceur » (2002); Bienvenue, Quand la jeunesse entre en scène (2003); Gauvreau, The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005); Bédard and Goyette, eds., Parole d’historiens (2006); Baillargeon, Brève histoire des femmes au Québec (2012).
nodes.scope_note: A research field defined by its object (Quebec and French Canada) and largely by its language. The Montreal school, Laval, the modernists and their critics are distinct and overlapping positions, not one school; Savard warns against treating ‘École de Québec’ as a unit. The post-1970 generation is called ‘modernist’ after Bédard and Goyette’s part title; Linteau calls it a ‘nouvelle histoire’; Rudin’s polemical name for it is used only in the normal-society debate strand. Annales influence is indirect and contested: Ouellet’s Labroussian economic history, Mandrou’s preface and Dechêne’s training in the Annales milieu are documented, while Linteau says his generation owed more to sociology and American historians. Groulx’s nationalism and clerical politics are historical subjects here, not the atlas’s categories. Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) and the Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution have their primary homes here. English-language historians of Quebec (Behiels, Dickinson, Young, Rudin, Greer) belong to the field. Acadian and francophone-minority historiography outside Quebec is only touched by Martel. New France encounter history with Indigenous peoples is in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history.

nodes.label: Canadian military history
nodes.date_label: Duguid’s only official volume 1938 · Stacey’s official histories 1955–70 · Nicholson’s replacement CEF history 1962 · Broken Promises 1977 · war-and-society studies 1986–93 · Walker on race and recruitment 1989 · Valour and the Horror broadcast and hearings 1992 · Vance 1997 · coverage through 2000, selected later works
nodes.description: Canadian military history has three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. Early work was largely official history, published by authority of the Minister of National Defence. Duguid’s official history of the Great War produced only one volume (1938); Nicholson’s Canadian Expeditionary Force (1962) replaced it. Stacey wrote volumes I (1955) and III (1960) of the Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War, and his Arms, Men and Governments (1970) made war policy a subject; Stanley’s Canada’s Soldiers (1954) called Canadians ‘an unmilitary people’. Conscription and French-Canadian participation recur, from Armstrong’s Crisis of Quebec (1937) to Granatstein and Hitsman’s Broken Promises (1977) and francophone histories of the 22nd Battalion (Gagnon 1986) and of bilingualism in the forces (Pariseau and Bernier 1987). From the 1980s war-and-society history turned to soldiers, veterans, psychiatry and women: Morton’s military and political histories (1981, 1985), veterans’ return (Morton and Wright 1987), battle exhaustion (Copp and McAndrew 1990) and Pierson on wartime womanhood (1986). Walker (1989) studied the enlistment of visible minorities, and Dempsey Prairie First Nations soldiers (1999). Popular history (Berton’s Vimy, 1986) and the CBC series The Valour and the Horror (1992), which led to Senate hearings and an ombudsman’s report, made military history a major public controversy. Vance’s Death So Noble (1997) treated the Great War as a cultural force in interwar memory. Cook (2002, 2006) showed that the records and narratives of Stacey’s officers were neither neutral nor unbiased.

III, The Victory Campaign (1960), Arms, Men and Governments (1970); Nicholson, Canadian Expeditionary Force (1962); Granatstein and Hitsman, Broken Promises (1977); Morton, Canada and War (1981), A Military History of Canada (1985), When Your Number’s Up (1993); Gagnon, Le 22e bataillon (1986); Pierson, “They’re Still Women After All” (1986); Berton, Vimy (1986); Morton and Wright, Winning the Second Battle (1987); Pariseau and Bernier, Les Canadiens français et le bilinguisme dans les Forces armées canadiennes, tome 1 (1987); Walker, “Race and Recruitment in World War I” (1989); Copp and McAndrew, Battle Exhaustion (1990); Bercuson and Wise, eds., The Valour and the Horror Revisited (1994); Dick, “‘The Valour and the Horror’ Continued” (1993); Gagnon (1995); Keshen, Propaganda and Censorship (1996); Vance, Death So Noble (1997); Dempsey, Warriors of the King (1999). Community and veteran histories: Ito, We Went to War (1984); Ruck, The Black Battalion (1987). Later: Cook, “Clio’s Soldiers” (2002) and Clio’s Warriors (2006); Keshen (2004); Rutherdale (2004); McKay and Swift, Warrior Nation (2012).
nodes.scope_note: A research field with three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. They are not successive stages; official historians also wrote policy history, and war-and-society historians also wrote operations. Popular history (Berton) and public controversy are included as part of the field’s public life, not as academic scholarship. Francophone work on conscription and French-Canadian participation is part of the field and meets Quebec historiography. Several roster people are treated mainly elsewhere (Stanley, Granatstein, Copp, Bercuson, Pierson, Vance); they appear for specific works. Imperial, naval and air histories and the Royal Military College tradition are thin in this selection. Critics of militarized memory (McKay and Swift) are after 2000. Black and Japanese-Canadian soldiers appear through Walker (1989, scholarly) and two community and veteran histories (Ruck 1987, Ito 1984). The Valour and the Horror controversy is a strand here, called a major public-history controversy on a contemporary witness (Dick 1993); Carr’s later treatment (CHR 2005) is unread, so it is not called a defining historiographical controversy.

nodes.label: Political, international & national history
nodes.date_label: Granatstein 1975, 1977, 1982 · Whitaker 1977 · Stacey 1977–81 · Bothwell, Drummond and English 1981 · Owram 1986 · Buckner 1993 · Whitaker and Marcuse 1994 · British World 2006 · CHA political history prizes first listed 2011 · Heaman's 'new political history' 2017 · coverage through 2000, selected later works
nodes.description: Research on the Canadian state, its parties, officials, wars and foreign relations, and the national syntheses built from them. Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975), of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) and of the Ottawa mandarins (1982), Whitaker's study of the Liberal party and the state (1977) and Owram's history of the intellectuals who argued for planning and reform (1986) examined how federal power was organized, staffed and justified. Stacey's history of external policies (1977, 1981), Hillmer and Granatstein's Empire to Umpire (1994) and Bothwell's Alliance and Illusion (2007) treated Canada's place in the world. Bothwell, Drummond and English's Canada since 1945 (1981) and Thompson and Seager's Centenary Series volume (1985) offered national syntheses; political biography (Brown on Borden, Bélanger on Laurier, English on Pearson) and Bliss's business history kept leaders and enterprise in view. Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1994) turned to the security state. Buckner's 1993 address, asking historians to restore the settlement colonies to imperial history, led to the British World volume (2006). Chapnick (2000, 2005) questioned the middle-power 'golden age'. Granatstein and Bliss also led the national side of the 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate. Since 2011 the CHA's political history prizes have rewarded a 'new political history' of state, tax and governance: Heaman on taxation (2017), Loo on forced relocation (2019), Bohaker on Anishinaabe governance (2020), and francophone studies of Hydro-Québec (Savard) and cultural policy (Harvey) that are recognized but not yet widely cited.

nodes.label: The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate
nodes.date_label: Roots: Cook 1967, Careless 1969 · Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' and the JCS replies 1991–92 · Strong-Boag's CHA address 1994 · Granatstein's book 1998 · CHR replies (McKillop, Palmer) and francophone reviews 1998–99 · CHR forum, Buckner, McKay and Osborne 2000 · Dummitt and Dawson 2009 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A quarrel among English-Canadian historians in the 1990s over whether national history had been lost, taught here as a moment in the profession's view of itself, not as current practice: few recent theses cite its texts. It had two phases. In 1991–92 Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' argued that intense specialization had replaced older historians' concern with explaining the country, and asked historians to remember that their subject was Canada. A 'Point-Counterpoint' in the same journal answered him: Gregory Kealey's class history was 'neither privatizing, nor sundering' (1992), and Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented. Strong-Boag's 1994 presidential address answered 'neo-conservative laments' by indicting an old history of white male elites. In 1998 Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? took the charge to a public audience. In the Canadian Historical Review McKillop (1999) argued that Granatstein's narrow national history was itself political legitimation, and Palmer offered a dissident view. Francophone reviewers answered too: Dubuc read a lament for political history; Dumont, an indictment of social historians built on wrong facts about Quebec schooling. It grew from the 'limited identities' of region, culture and class that Cook named (1967) and Careless popularized (1969). In 2000 Létourneau proposed a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions, Cook called identities contingent and multiple, Buckner revisited limited identities, and McKay offered the liberal order framework as a way past the impasse. Dummitt and Dawson (2009) sought to move beyond political-versus-social history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969); Reid (1987); Buckner (1988). Phase one: Bliss, "Privatizing the Mind" (1991–92), answered in the JCS Point-Counterpoint by G. Kealey (1992) and L. Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag (1992); Strong-Boag, "Contested Space" (1994). Phase two: Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), answered in the CHR by McKillop, "A View from the Trenches" (1999) and Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches" (1999); Strong-Boag's review (1999); francophone reviews by Dionne (RHAF 1998), Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc (BHP 1999) and Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999). Reassessments: Létourneau and the CHR forum (2000); Cook, "Identities Are Not Like Hats" (2000); Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000); McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework" (2000); Osborne (2000). Later: Dummitt and Dawson, eds., Contesting Clio's Craft (2009); Hamilton (2012).
nodes.scope_note: A debate entry measured through its texts, not its people, and written as a teaching entry about the profession's self-understanding rather than current practice: any core debate text is cited by 34 of 1,303 strict 2009–2026 History PhDs (2.6%), falling to 2.0% in 2020–26. It has two phases: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies (1991–92), and Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies (1998–99); the 1992 JCS pieces answer Bliss, not Who Killed Canadian History?. Most participants' citations in the PhD corpus come from their other work. Bliss and Granatstein's scholarship is in Political, international & national history; Bliss's main entry is Political, international & national history; this entry keeps his debate row. The replying fields are proposed as Canadian working-class history, Canadian women's & gender history and Canadian regional history. Several replies are characterized by title only (Gregory Kealey 1992; Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag 1992; Palmer 1999). The exchange among the main protagonists was English-Canadian, but francophone historians answered Granatstein in RHAF, the Bulletin d'histoire politique and the CHA Bulletin (1998–99); no francophone reply to Bliss was found. Létourneau's 2000 CHR essay is the francophone voice in the 2000 reassessments. Quebec's own debate over national and political history (the BHP from 1992, Bélanger 1997, later the 2006–07 school programme) ran separately; its checked texts do not cite Bliss or Granatstein, and it is related here only by comparison. Osborne's school-history essay links to history education, which the atlas does not treat as an entry.

strands.title: Roots: limited identities
strands.focus: Cook's phrase (1967) and Careless's programme (1969) made region, culture and class the frame; Buckner (1988) judged it premature to abandon; Reid (1987) records the first worries about fragmentation. The debate grows out of this, not out of the 1990s alone.

Buckner, "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship: An Atlantic Provinces Perspective," Journal of Canadian Studies 23, no. 1–2 (1988): 177–198.; John G. Reid, "Towards the Elusive Synthesis: The Atlantic Provinces in Recent General Treatments of Canadian History," Acadiensis 16, no. 2 (1987): 107ff.

strands.title: Phase one, 1991–92: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies
strands.focus: Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (JCS 26:4, 1991–92): specialization had displaced older historians' concern with explaining the country (abstract). A 'Point-Counterpoint' in JCS 27:2 (1992) answered him with 'counter-positions … on the centralist views of Canadian history as articulated by Michael Bliss' (MUSE framing): Gregory Kealey defended class analysis as 'neither privatizing, nor sundering'; Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented (both title level). Strong-Boag's 1994 CHA address answered 'neo-conservative laments' (abstract). These pieces predate Who Killed Canadian History? and are not replies to it.

strands.title: Phase two, 1998–99: Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies
strands.focus: Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), which named the debate, took the charge to a public audience (as McKillop summarizes it: academic historians had abandoned a national past for 'overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history'). In the CHR McKillop (80:2, June 1999) argued that Granatstein miscasts the scholar as citizen and that his national history is itself political legitimation; Palmer (80:4, December 1999) offered 'a dissident view' (title level). Strong-Boag reviewed the book in Historical Studies in Education (1999; unread). Francophone historians answered the book too, as reviewers: Dionne in RHAF (1998); Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc in the BHP (1999), Dubuc reading it as a lament for political history as a discipline (first page); and Dumont in the CHA Bulletin (1999, read in full), who corrected its claims about Quebec schooling and called it a fierce indictment of social historians. No francophone reply to Bliss was found.

nodes.label: Canadian regional history
nodes.date_label: Morton's Manitoba 1957 · Ormsby's British Columbia 1958 · Craig's Upper Canada 1963 · 'limited identities' 1967–69 · Acadiensis 1971 · Acheson 1972 · Forbes 1979 · Friesen 1984 · Barman 1991 · reassessments 2000 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Histories of Canada's regions as places with their own economies, societies and identities rather than as peripheries of a central-Canadian story. Provincial syntheses such as Morton's Manitoba (1957) and Ormsby's British Columbia (1958) preceded the 'limited identities' argument: Cook (1967) suggested that Canadianism might be found in regional, ethnic and class identities, and Careless (1969) made the phrase a programme. Acadiensis was revived in 1971 (Windsor's initiative; Buckner editor), its first editorial faulting historians 'obsessed with the great "national" themes'. Acheson (1972) traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy and its subordination to Montreal capital, and Forbes studied the Maritime Rights movement (1979). Friesen (1984), Barman (1991), Conrad and Hiller (2001) and Waiser (2005) wrote regional syntheses, while Owram, Carter and Harris tied western and Pacific history to expansionist ideas, reserve policy and colonial geography. Ontario had provincial histories of its own (Craig 1963; Nelles 1974; McCalla 1993). Acadia became a growing Atlantic literature: Griffiths on Acadian history and identity (1992, 2005), Plank and Faragher on conquest and expulsion (2001, 2005), and Reid, Basque and colleagues on 1710 (2004). Francophone regional history worked at other scales: Painchaud on the Church and French Prairie settlement (a 1970s study, published posthumously in 1987), Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001), and Quebec's intraprovincial regional histories, which Harvey contrasts with interprovincial regionalism. By 2000 McKay asked whether 'region' could hold the new histories of gender, ethnicity and community, and Buckner revisited limited identities.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Morton, Manitoba (1957); Ormsby, British Columbia (1958); Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969) and Frontier and Metropolis (1989); Buckner, "Acadiensis II" (1971), (1988) and (2000); Acheson, "The National Policy and the Industrialization of the Maritimes" (1972); Forbes, The Maritime Rights Movement (1979); Owram, Promise of Eden (1980); Craig, Upper Canada (1963); Nelles, The Politics of Development (1974); Drummond, Progress without Planning (1987); McCalla, Planting the Province (1993); Friesen, The Canadian Prairies (1984); Painchaud, Un rêve français dans le peuplement de la Prairie (1987, posthumous); Griffiths, The Contexts of Acadian History (1992) and From Migrant to Acadian (2005); Plank, An Unsettled Conquest (2001); Landry and Lang, Histoire de l'Acadie (2001); Faragher, A Great and Noble Scheme (2005); Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Barman, The West Beyond the West (1991); Harris, The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997); Stonechild and Waiser, Loyal till Death (1997); Conrad and Hiller, Atlantic Canada (2001); Reid, Basque et al., The "Conquest" of Acadia (2004); Waiser, Saskatchewan (2005); Baskerville, Sites of Power (2005); Reimer, Writing British Columbia History (2009); Sandwell, Contesting Rural Space (2005); Harvey (2006). Critique: McKay, "A Note on 'Region'" (2000).
nodes.scope_note: A research field for Canada's regions (the Prairie West, British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces including Acadia, and Ontario) and the limited-identities argument. Provincial syntheses, regional economic history, rural history and regional identity are distinct strands. Indigenous and settler-colonial histories of the West and British Columbia overlap strongly (Carter, Harris) and are primarily placed in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history, Settler colonialism and environment. Ontario has a strand of provincial syntheses and economic histories chosen by PhD citation counts; Acadia has its own Atlantic strand. The North and Newfoundland are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 titles) and get only this note. Quebec's regional history appears only as a contrast of scale. Roster inclusion does not imply that historians accepted "limited identities".

strands.title: Acadia (Atlantic)
strands.focus: Acadia before and after the expulsion of 1755. In the PhD corpus this is a substantial and rising literature: 101 of 1,303 PhDs (2009–2026) cite Acadian history works, 5.1% in 2009–14 and 8.9% in 2020–26, 23 of them at francophone universities. Griffiths, an authority on pre-1755 Acadia, wrote on its contexts to 1784 (1992) and the emergence of Acadian identity (2005); Plank (2001) and Faragher (2005) studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia and the expulsion; Reid, Basque and colleagues read the 1710 conquest from imperial, Acadian and Mi'kmaw perspectives (2004). Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001) is a francophone university synthesis of Maritime Acadia over four centuries that sets out to recount the experience of the whole Acadian people, not only its elite. Most of these works are later readings, after 2000. Readers of this literature also engage Quebec historiography (lift 3.2): see the comparison with Quebec historiography.

nodes.label: Canada’s 1960s
nodes.date_label: Early accounts: Kostash 1980, Levitt 1984 · Behiels 1985 · Owram 1996 · Igartua 2006 · Palmer, Warren 2008–09 · Mills 2010 · Debating Dissent 2012 · coverage through 2000; selected later readings
nodes.description: Historical writing that treats Canada's long 1960s as a subject in its own right: the baby boom and youth revolt, the New Left and labour militancy, Quebec's Quiet Revolution and its radicalisms, rights movements, decolonization and Red Power, and the remaking of national identity. Early book-length accounts include Kostash's interview-based history of her own generation (1980) and Levitt (1984). Doug Owram's Born at the Right Time (1996) followed the baby-boom generation from suburb and school to counterculture and youth radicalism. José Igartua's The Other Quiet Revolution (2006) traced English Canada's British self-definition giving way to a civic, rights-based identity, and Dominique Clément studied its rights associations. Bryan Palmer's Canada's 1960s (2009) read the decade through the ironies of national identity, with chapters on wildcat strikes, the New Left, Quebec and the 'discovery' of the 'Indian'. Sean Mills's The Empire Within (2010) traced postcolonial thought in Montreal activism, and David Austin race, sex and security there. Campbell, Clément and Kealey's Debating Dissent (2012) and Ian Milligan's Rebel Youth (2014), on young workers and New Leftists, widened the field. Francophone historians debate continuity and rupture. Michael Behiels, E.-Martin Meunier and Jean-Philippe Warren, and Louise Bienvenue found the Quiet Revolution's roots in postwar liberalism and in Catholic Action, against its own story of a 'grande noirceur'. Warren's Une douce anarchie (2008) historicized the student revolt of 1968. It is a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram, Palmer, Mills, Igartua), not a school like the atlas's New Left entry.

Comparison: Marwick, The Sixties (1998).
nodes.scope_note: A research field defined by its subject, the long 1960s (roughly late 1950s to early 1970s), not by a method or school. It replaces the "postwar Canada" data cluster (user, 2026-10-12: "1960s is its own thing"). Distinguish the atlas's New Left entry (radical historians as a school) from histories of the New Left as a movement. The Quebec strand overlaps Quebec historiography and the Catholic Action revision in religion history; those works remain treated mainly there. Register: a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram 71 and Palmer 67 citing PhDs; Mills; Igartua), with engagement modestly falling (ratio 0.78; fixed panel 0.81), not a school. Black Canadian sixties history: Austin (2013) is a later reading; before 2000 the only verified work is a contemporary participants' collection (Forsythe, ed., 1971), so pre-2000 scholarly coverage is a gap.

nodes.label: Settler colonialism
nodes.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999 · coverage through 2000; selected later readings: Wolfe 2006, Veracini 2010, journal 2011, critiques 2013–20; field chronology unresolved
nodes.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) and “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. (2005); Veracini, Settler Colonialism (2010) and Settler Colonial Studies (2011). Read with Coulthard (2014), A. Simpson (2014), L. B. Simpson (2011, 2017), Byrd (2011) and Tuck and Yang (2012). Canadian historiography: Carter (1990, 2008), Harris (2002, 2004, 2020), Perry (2001), Regan (2010), Daschuk (2013), Battell Lowman and Barker (2015), Burrill (2019). Critiques: Macoun and Strakosch (2013), Rowse (2014), Kauanui (2016), Greer (2019), Shoemaker (2019), Konishi (2019), Garba and Sorentino (2020).
nodes.scope_note: A selective research field whose theoretical consolidation came mostly after 2000; the entry covers its roots through 2000 and cites selected later works as readings. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1983 and 1995 are earlier settler-society witnesses, not the field's origin; Wolfe 1999 is the only selected milestone inside 1920–2000. Naming and consolidation fall after 2000; neither endpoint bounds the field. Drawn to the atlas coverage limit (2000); later works are cited readings, not registered extension coverage (revision 1.128).

sources.citation: James W. St. G. Walker, "Allegories and Orientations in African-Canadian Historiography: The Spirit of Africville," Dalhousie Review 77, no. 2 (1997): 155–178.

verification.note: Full text read. Walker identifies five "orientations" (not schools) in African-Canadian historiography, distinguished by the role assigned to Black people: Black Clients (focus on white justice and philanthropy), Black Victims, Black Achievers, Black Community (which coincided with the social history movement) and, in the 1990s, Black Survivors. Africville serves as allegory for the African-Canadian experience. Note: the request cited this as CHR 1999; the checked record is Dalhousie Review 1997. Re-read 2026-10-12 for this draft: Clients (Landon, Riddell; Stouffer 1992), Victims (Silverman 1985; "American scholars pointed the finger at the racist reality lurking behind the North Star mythology"), Achievers, Community (Black Power, Black pride, social history; Winks said The Black Loyalists ended the "victims" school), Survivors (Brand 1991). About 80 articles, 50 books and 40 graduate theses in two decades; black women receiving increasing attention. The further-reading list was used to corroborate several records. Checked against: DalSpace (Dalhousie) repository record and full-text PDF.
